item.title: Learning of LPV Models With Linear Fractional Representations: Initialization, Optimization, and Conditioning
item.description: arXiv:2611.14668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) models with Linear Fractional Representation (LFR) can describe a wide class of nonlinear systems with a control-friendly structure. However, identifying these models together with their scheduling map from input-output data requires solving a non-convex optimization problem that is highly sensitive to initialization. Consequently, existing methods often rely on many random initializations. Instead, our work proposes an initialization strategy based on the Best Linear Approximator (BLA). Furthermore, motivated by an analysis of the impact of rational-dependency LPV-LFR models on the conditioning of the non-convex cost, two multiple shooting methods that improve the conditioning, unconstrained multiple shooting (UMS) and encoder-based multiple shooting (EBMS), are compared. The initialization and multiple shooting methods are evaluated on a nonlinear mass-spring-damper example, showing that BLA initialization consistently yields accurate results, whereas random initialization has a large spread. The results also show that both UMS and EBMS reduce the spread for randomly initialized models. UMS is simple to tune and well suited to few sub-records, whereas EBMS can exploit many short sub-records to further improve conditioning, at the cost of training an encoder and tuning additional hyperparameters.
item.dc:creator: Roel Drenth, Maarten Schoukens, Roland T\'oth

item.title: A Three-Stage Unsupervised Online Physics-Informed Neural Network for Microgrid Optimal Power Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.14716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal allocation of generators is a key challenge in power systems to achieve economical dispatch while satisfying operational constraints. Conventional optimization techniques can be computationally expensive, limiting their applicability in real-time environments, and neural networks often require offline retraining under new operating conditions. This paper proposes a three-stage unsupervised online physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for optimal power flow (OPF). Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework satisfies load demand and system constraints while achieving a $43,665 lower operating cost than fmincon-based optimization under the same operating conditions. The training process analysis further demonstrate the framework's ability to adapt its parameters online to variations in load demand and renewable generation in real time.
item.dc:creator: Abinash Giri, Yi Hu

item.title: U.S. Data Center Growth Through 2030: A Critical Review of Grid Adequacy and Transmission Expansion Planning
item.description: arXiv:2611.14759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growth of large data centers raises questions about both supply adequacy and the suitability of load representations used in connection studies. This paper critically reviews the U.S. demand, generation, and transmission outlook through 2030 and examines the implications for transmission expansion planning (TEP). Comparison of public forecasts highlights distinctions among annual average demand, peak demand, and grid connection capacity. National generating-capacity totals cannot establish a dependable surplus because resource availability, regional adequacy, transmission constraints, and project timing determine supply capability. Recent grid events and published dynamic studies demonstrate that faults can trigger substantial data-center transfers to backup supply, followed by delayed or coordinated demand recovery. These behaviors require appropriate representation within the conventional planning framework, alongside assessment of the requested maximum grid import. The selected literature reveals limited integration of validated data-center dynamic models into the technical screening and economic comparison of expansion alternatives. The review identifies the need to establish whether fault response and recovery change feasible connection capacity, required reinforcement, or the preferred transmission investment.
item.dc:creator: Babak Porkar, Mona Ghassemi

item.title: An Inductively Assisted N :1 Switched-Capacitor Ladder Converter
item.description: arXiv:2611.14778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes an inductively assisted N:1 switched-capacitor ladder buck (D-SCLB) converter that replaces the output-side switch in the bottom half-bridge of an N:1 SCLB with a small inductor placed in parallel with the ladder capacitors during the demagnetization phase. The flying capacitors share the load current delivery, lowering the average inductor current to (1-M)Iout and enabling continuous regulation with M=D/(N-1+D). A closed-form output-impedance model, valid for arbitrary N under both optimal and uniform switch sizing, is derived and compared against SC, SCLB, FCMC, and DPSC topologies. For a 4:1 48V-to-PoL design, the D-SCLB reduces the average inductor current by up to 20% and improves the equivalent output impedance by up to 30% relative to the SCLB. Two hardware prototypes on a low-cost two-layer PCB achieve a peak efficiency of 96.2%, with the D-SCLB using 49% smaller inductor volume than the SCLB at comparable efficiency. Model predictions agree with measurements to within 1.5% under heavy load.
item.dc:creator: Sandeep Reddy Kukunuru, M Mahmudul Hasan Sajeeb, Rohit Reddy Karnaty, Loai G. Salem

item.title: AgentiGrid: Agentic AI for Steady State and Transient Studies
item.description: arXiv:2611.14854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As power systems worldwide struggle to meet in- creasing loads or higher penetration of inverter based resources, dynamic studies become of increasing importance. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities allows to automate some of these resource intensive studies. Coupled with parallel computing, AI is a promising technology to conduct transient and stability studies on an unprecedented scale. This study provides a proof of concept agentic AI capable of parallel or sequential execution of phasor domain studies for a 10,000 bus system. The agent first executes a standalone simulation of a three phase symmetric fault and then executes a series of actions, by first adding a large load to a bus and then applying the fault to the same bus to stress the system. The results of the agentic simulation are consistent with human counterfactual across four vendor backends.
item.dc:creator: Eve Tsybina, Selma Grebovic, Samim Konjicija, Kaleb Brunhoeber, Slaven Peles

item.title: Beyond Yes or No: Grading Observability of Power System Dynamic States with Symbolic Coefficients
item.description: arXiv:2611.14890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph-based observability analysis runs in seconds where Lie-derivative tests take hours, but it answers only one question: is the system observable or not. It cannot say how well a given set of measurements supports state reconstruction. This paper extends the graph-based approach with symbolic observability coefficients computed from a symbolic Jacobian of the state-space equations, in which every dependency is classified as constant, nonlinear polynomial, or rational. We show that the coefficient tracks the analytical observability determinant of the Lie-derivative approach: it is zero when the determinant vanishes, lies strictly between zero and one when the determinant depends on the state, and equals one when the determinant is a nonzero constant. We apply the method to a seven-state synchronous machine and to the 21-state Western System Coordinating Council nine-bus system under several synchrophasor measurement configurations. On the nine-bus system, the coefficient grows from 0.0952 with one PMU to 0.1905 with two and 0.2857 with three, and the whole analysis runs in under five seconds. Configurations with the same number of PMUs receive the same coefficient, yet an unscented Kalman filter estimates the states with different accuracy for each. The symbolic coefficient therefore grades measurement sets beyond identifying root strongly connected components, while telling PMU locations apart still requires the numerical parameters of the system.
item.dc:creator: Akhila Kandivalasa, Marcos Netto

item.title: Inverse-Optimal Fixed-Time Integral Reinforcement Learning for Unknown Nonlinear Leader-Follower Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.14927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a distributed inverse-optimal fixed-time integral reinforcement learning framework for unknown nonlinear leader-follower multi-agent systems. The proposed method first reconstructs the unknown agent dynamics from finite integral data. Based on the identified dynamics, a distributed inverse-optimal formulation is constructed by prescribing a desired fixed-time value function and recovering a compatible running cost. A critic-only integral reinforcement learning architecture is then developed using current integral data and finitely informative experience-replay data, thereby avoiding the persistent-excitation requirement. Practical fixed-time convergence of the critic-weight errors is established in the presence of identification and function-approximation residuals. Finally, a network-level composite Lyapunov analysis proves practical fixed-time leader-following consensus of the true unknown nonlinear multi-agent system. Numerical simulations are provided to validate the developed theory.
item.dc:creator: Tien Dat Vu, Minh Doan

item.title: LLM-Enhanced Deep Reinforcement Learning with Human-in-the-Loop Calibration for Real-Time Optimal Power Flow
item.description: arXiv:2611.15003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time optimal power flow (RT-OPF) requires fast and reliable decision-making under time-varying operating conditions. However, many practical operating preferences and safety related requirements are difficult to encode using conventional numerical rewards alone, which limits the effectiveness and controllability of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for RT-OPF. To address this issue, this paper proposes an LLM-enhanced DRL framework with human-in-the-loop (HITL) for RT-OPF. The proposed method augments the physics-based reward with sparse language evaluative feedback during offline training, so that semantic operational requirements can be incorporated into policy learning. To improve reliability in RT-OPF, a selective HITL calibration mechanism is further introduced to inspect and correct questionable LLM judgments before they continuously shape the learning process. Case studies on the IEEE 30-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems show that LLM feedback improves policy safety over vanilla TD3, while further HITL calibration achieves the best overall performance and more stable training behavior. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining language guidance and expert calibration for RT-OPF.
item.dc:creator: Jiayang Tu, Bozhen Jiang, Bojun Du, Yunxiao Ling, Ershun Du, Qin Wang

item.title: TDMOpt: LLM-Driven Cross-layer Dispatch for Transmission-Distribution-Microgrid Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.15012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coordinating transmission networks, distribution networks, and microgrids enables distributed flexibility to support renewable energy integration and low-carbon operation. However, heterogeneous resources, cross-layer coupling, and varying operating requirements complicate the selection of models and coordination schemes that are both physically adequate and computationally tractable. This paper proposes TDMOpt, a LLM-driven multi-agent framework that replaces fixed modeling configurations with adaptive model composition. A layered component library provides executable network, resource, objective, constraint, and coordination models. Guided by retrieved physics and component knowledge, the agents infer specific modeling requirements and jointly select compatible components across layers according to operating conditions and computational budgets. The model compositions undergo independent AC power flow validation, since feasibility in a simplified formulation does not ensure compliance with physical network limits. A refinement mechanism interprets numerical feedback to identify modeling requirements for reconsideration and revise relevant component selections. Case studies on different scale systems illustrate the framework's ability to adapt model combinations and obtain validated dispatch solutions through targeted refinement under varying operating conditions.
item.dc:creator: Jiayang Tu, Bojun Du, Jijun Shui, Ershun Du, Qin Wang

item.title: Metropolis Random Walks Escape Deep Basins Faster in Higher Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.15086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulated Annealing (SA) is a widely used stochastic optimization algorithm. It is of great interest to understand how its ability to escape local minima at a fixed temperature depends on geometry and dimension. In prior work, we derived closed-form expressions for the expected basin escape time of a constant-temperature SA process on a one-dimensional piecewise-linear landscape. In this paper, we extend the analysis to $D$-dimensional cubic basins defined by the infinity-norm energy $V(x)=\|x\|_\infty$. The walk proposes nearest-neighbor moves uniformly and escapes upon first reaching the outer shell, that is, any site with $\|x\|_\infty=N$. We construct a one-dimensional birth-death shell-quotient chain by collapsing each concentric shell in the Metropolis electrical network to a single node while retaining its total stationary mass. We derive a closed-form expression for the mean escape time $Q_D(N)$ of this shell-quotient chain as a function of the acceptance probability $p$, the basin depth $N$, and the dimension $D$. For fixed $D$ and fixed $0<p<1$, the quotient escape time scales as $\Theta(\alpha^N/N^{D-1})$ as $N\to\infty$, where $\alpha=1/p$. Relative to $D=1$, this gives an asymptotic speedup of order $N^{D-1}$ within this family of cubic basins. We prove that the true Metropolis mean escape time $H_D(N)$, without shell averaging, has the same $\Theta(\alpha^N/N^{D-1})$ scaling, establishing a lower bound via Rayleigh monotonicity and a matching upper bound through an explicit low-energy flow construction using Thomson's principle. Numerical solutions that exploit the walk's symmetries quantify the discrepancy between the quotient and true-chain means for $D=1,2,3$.
item.dc:creator: Hansini Ramachandran, Bhaskar Krishnamachari

item.title: Backstepping-Forwarding Design for Hyperbolic PIDE-ODE Systems with Distributed Interconnection and an Arbitrarily Large Input Delay
item.description: arXiv:2611.15123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies first-order hyperbolic partial integro-differential equation (PIDE) and ordinary differential equation (ODE) cascades with distributed interconnection and an arbitrarily large known constant input delay. Within the backstepping--forwarding framework, a forwarding-type transformation is designed to reduce the distributed interconnection to an equivalent boundary-coupled Dirichlet cascade without requiring the PIDE to be open-loop stable. A subsequent backstepping design stabilizes the PIDE and the ODE while compensating for the input delay. Incompatible boundary conditions in the delay-compensation kernel equations may produce discontinuities along characteristic lines. We determine their jump locations and amplitudes and prove that the interface terms cancel when deriving the target equations, so the kernel discontinuities do not change the target system. Closed-loop exponential stability is established without additional plant restrictions to ensure kernel continuity. A numerical example illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
item.dc:creator: Yidan Cao, Xiang Xu, Lu Liu

item.title: Sim-to-Real Powertrain Vibration Control via Model-Based Assisted Domain-Randomized Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.15133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controllers designed from nominal models often degrade on mechanical systems with nonlinearities and parametric variations, such as automotive powertrains with backlash. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with domain randomization can acquire robustness to such model discrepancies, but wide randomization destabilizes training and yields conservative policies, and experimental transfer of such policies has rarely been demonstrated in vibration control. This paper presents model-based controller assisted domain randomization (MBCADR), a framework that integrates model-based control into domain-randomized DRL. An $H_{2}$ controller designed from the nominal model supplies a baseline action, while a residual policy trained with twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient under randomized dynamics compensates for nonlinearities and uncertainties. This model-based assistance relieves the agent of synthesizing the entire control input, thereby stabilizing training under extensive randomization. For each realization of the uncertain parameters, the augmented plant--controller state is shown to be a Markov state of the closed loop, so that domain-randomized training is rigorously formulated as policy optimization over a parameterized family of Markov decision processes. A Lyapunov-based stability analysis further derives a forward-invariant set and an explicit ultimate bound, in which the learned action enters only through its saturation level. Monte Carlo simulations with multiple training seeds show that MBCADR reduces performance variability compared with either component alone. Experiments on a powertrain test bench with backlash, using the simulation-trained policy on an embedded processor without further tuning, confirm successful sim-to-real transfer.
item.dc:creator: Heisei Yonezawa, Ansei Yonezawa, Itsuro Kajiwara

item.title: Low-Data OOD Prediction of SAW Resonators with Simulation-Compensated Transfer Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.15140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators are foundational to modern radio-frequency (RF) front-end architectures. However, models trained on limited fabricated devices generalize poorly to unmeasured design regions because of process-induced variations, while finite-element method (FEM) simulations, although inexpensive, exhibit systematic offsets from measurements. To predict device performance before physical prototyping, this work presents a simulation-compensated transfer-learning framework that uses computationally efficient 2.5-D FEM simulations as physics-based anchors and learns their calibration to the measurement domain. Using 4,236 measured lithium tantalate (LiTaO3) SAW resonators and 816 unique simulated configurations, five transfer strategies are systematically benchmarked under seven out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols spanning frequency, geometry, and material shifts. The proposed framework reduces OOD prediction error by 83.54% on average (up to 97.57%) relative to the Measurement-only baseline, with the best strategy selected per case, and raises the pooled R2 of frequency prediction to 1.000, offering an economically scalable route toward physics-guided, fabrication-aware machine learning for microelectromechanical-system (MEMS) acoustic-device design.
item.dc:creator: Zhijie Ma, Xingyu Liu, Shuhan Chen, Fangsheng Qian, Junyan Zheng, Nan Jun Kim, Taek Joo Lee, Hyung Kook Yang, Yansong Yang

item.title: When Does Learned Constraint Selection Pay in Security-Constrained Optimisation? A Boundary Map from SCOPF to Unit Commitment
item.description: arXiv:2611.15142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning-to-optimise methods for security-constrained optimal power flow (SCOPF) predict the security constraints that bind on each instance and solve only the reduced problem, with reported speed-ups of two to four orders of magnitude over the full problem. We ask whether learned selection beats the strongest learning-free alternative: a fixed umbrella set enforcing every constraint observed to bind in training. Our criterion, the price of a spare, answers this in advance: an enforced but inactive constraint is free, so the umbrella is exactly optimal wherever feasible, and learning can pay only where a spare decision carries a price. We test it systematically, including every PGLib-OPF network up to 10,000 buses. For SCOPF on a fixed network the umbrella is never beaten: its median size is five constraints across 43 networks, with no size trend, and our selector, while reproducing speed-ups of published magnitude (about x80,000 at case500), gains at most 0.25 ms over the umbrella and violates constraints on 4-5% of instances. Configuration diversity can break the umbrella's coverage on a small, densely meshed network but not at 2,000 buses, and we certify coverage with conformal risk control. In unit commitment, where a spare has a price, a static commitment loses 4-12% out of sample, and a predict-repair-reduce pipeline recovers it (cost gap 0.2-2.9%, fully feasible, 16-161x faster than the MILP). In our experiments, whether learning pays depends not on problem size but on whether a spare carries a price.
item.dc:creator: Milad Kazemi, Behzad Kazemtabrizi

item.title: Quantum Computing in Power Systems:Current Landscape and Future Roadmap with AI
item.description: arXiv:2611.15171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern power systems are characterized by greater penetration of renewable energy resources, extensive use of power electronics, and more diverse loads. This leads to a dramatic increase in computational complexity, which, in turn, compromises solution efficiency and fails to satisfy the real time demands of system analysis. Recently, quantum computing techniques, attributed to their unique physical properties, such as superposition and entanglement, hold the potential to offer new solutions for power systems. To this end, this paper not only provides a comprehensive landscape of quantum computing in power systems, but also investigates its roadmap with AI enabled evolution. This paper begins with an introduction to the fundamental concepts of quantum computing, followed by a review of several approaches to power system simulation and optimization. Subsequently, we further investigate the potential quantum AI-enabled evolution in power systems. In addition, the current development of quantum software and hardware platforms is elaborated. Finally, this paper synthesizes the prevailing challenges and prospects for future research directions.
item.dc:creator: Yijun Xu, Yongbing Yao, Wei Gu, Chengjun Liu, Qi Lou, Lamine Mili, Mohammadreza Saghafi, Mert Korkali, Shuai Lu

item.title: Towards Efficient Edge AI for Power Flow in Renewable-Rich Grids with Volt/VAR Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.15181v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI models of the power grid must capture how wind and solar plants support the voltage, adjusting their reactive power to the local voltage along a grid-code Q(V) characteristic. This research examines whether grid foundation models, fast neural network models for power-flow analysis, can represent this behaviour. We introduce the Q(V) bus, a new bus type for the open-source GridFM GraphKit, whose physics decoder evaluates the reactive injection from the plant characteristic at the predicted voltage in every correction step. Training data comprise 7882 hourly operating points of a modified IEEE 118-bus system, matched to Energinet DK1/DK2 measurements and solved with pandapower. Compared with a physics-informed baseline that represents the parks as negative load, the Q(V) bus lowers the voltage-magnitude RMSE 2.3-fold, reduces the power-balance mismatch at the parks from 25 to 0.66 MVA, and raises the F1 score for voltage-band violations from 0.40 to 0.76. An ablation over five configurations shows that the Q(V) bus type provides the accuracy and the physics loss provides the power balance. For edge monitoring, we distil the trained $2.0\times10^{7}$-parameter model into students of $6\times10^{5}$ and $1.3\times10^{6}$ parameters; a flat-start initialisation prevents their collapse into an incorrect low-voltage state in which the characteristic saturates. With output distillation, the 12-step student reaches 1.4 times the teacher's error and, for edge inference on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (15 W), solves an hourly scenario in 12.2 ms, within the 20 ms synchrophasor interval.
item.dc:creator: Shahariya R. R. Puthanpurayil (AAU Energy, Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark), Vlad A. Sanduleac (National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest, Bucharest, Romania), Remus Teodorescu (AAU Energy, Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark)

item.title: Algorithms for Robust Dedicated Actuator Placement
item.description: arXiv:2611.15205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study dedicated actuators installed at distinct states of a structured linear system. Failures remove actuators but preserve states and state arcs. For unit costs and one failure, an exact source-quota relaxation followed by maximum matching in a \emph{common-repair graph} yields a $3/2$-approximation on arbitrary directed state graphs using $O(n^3)$ elementary graph operations. The analysis combines fundamental cocircuit unions with the Tutte--Berge formula. For multiple failures, we give an exact algorithm fixed-parameter tractable in the maximum-matching deficiency and failure budget, independently of the number of source strongly connected components. The underlying result solves resilient matroid spanning with an arbitrary number of disjoint unit-cost quota constraints. We also establish an exact weighted spanning algorithm for safe and vulnerable elements in the independence-oracle model, with an application to strongly connected state graphs.
item.dc:creator: Qichao Wang, Daoyu Dong

item.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Dissipativity for Distributed Power-System Stability Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.15240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compositional dissipativity is attractive for large-scale interconnected systems, but its application to modern heterogeneous power systems is limited by conservative descriptions of nodal dissipativity and inefficient distributed implementation. This paper introduces a common first-order dynamic lifting of the physical voltage-current port, providing an enriched dissipativity representation that captures complementary frequency-dependent energy behavior while preserving network composability. The resulting representation accommodates heterogeneous power system buses within a unified dissipativity description and enables less conservative compositional stability analysis. A centralized stability-certification problem is then formulated and solved through a dual-guided column-generation scheme. Its matrix dual reveals the network-critical dissipation direction, which guides parallel local certificate generation toward the current system bottleneck. This leads to a distributed Network-Critical Margin Exchange (NCME) method with early stability certification. Case studies demonstrate substantially reduced conservatism of the dynamic-port formulation and improved computational and communication scalability of NCME for heterogeneous power systems.
item.dc:creator: Xi Ru, Xiaoyu Peng, Feng Liu

item.title: Fundamental Limits of Data-Driven Predictive Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.15289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) has attracted substantial interest, and many variants have been proposed; however, comparatively less is known about the statistical closed-loop performance of these methods and the fundamental limits they are subject to. In this contribution, we apply the statistical decision framework developed in our earlier work to study fundamental limits of DDPC. The performance of a data-driven controller is measured by its risk, the expected deterioration in control performance relative to an oracle model-based controller at a given system, and by its total risk that measures the overall performance across all systems of interest. Lower bounds on these risks are derived using the bias-variance decomposition and the Cramer-Rao inequality. In particular, a lower bound on the total risk is obtained by a calculus-of-variations method. This bound applies to any DDPC design, thereby quantifying unavoidable performance limitations and providing a benchmark for assessing existing DDPC methods. In an illustrative example, we compare the risks of certainty-equivalence model predictive control, subspace predictive control, and data-enabled predictive control with the derived lower bounds, providing a quantitative performance assessment of these methods and some guidance on tuning regularization parameters in DDPC.
item.dc:creator: Jiabao He, Feiran Zhao, Yushan Li, Yue Ju, Florian D\"orfler, H{\aa}kan Hjalmarsson

item.title: Agreement Is Not Assurance: Evidence-Independent Safety Gates for Agentic AI in DER-Rich Distribution Grids
item.description: arXiv:2611.15363v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-based safety gates for large language model (LLM) agents can approve unsafe actions when the agent and gate rely on the same corrupted measurements or network records. We formulate this shared-evidence failure for voltage-constrained distributed energy resource (DER) export decisions and analyze how nearly critical DER telemetry can bias state estimation while evading residual-based bad-data detection. We propose evidence-independent verification (EIV), which combines advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) voltage readings, measurement selection based on predicted voltage rise, and bounded physical probes. An IEEE 123-bus hidden-truth testbed evaluates 1,654 near-limit requests under telemetry attacks and record errors. For telemetry attacks targeting the nominal gate, an AC-twin gate with bad-data detection approved 95% of unsafe requests, compared with 3.1% for EIV; EIV rejected 22% of safe clean requests. At matched false-rejection settings, direct AMI checks outperformed incorporating the same readings into state estimation. Gate-targeted attacks exposed a vulnerability in telemetry-based response prediction. Command-based prediction removed that route, but targeted attacks on fresh validation cases still produced a 20% unsafe-approval rate under the tested attack pool. LLM agents frequently sought independent evidence voluntarily, but injected instructions and phase-label errors caused unsafe decisions. When offered the EIV checker as a tool, they used it in 93-100% of episodes; mandatory use did not reduce observed violations, which primarily reflected checker errors. These results distinguish enforcement of verification from reliability of the verifier itself.
item.dc:creator: Qianxue Xia

item.title: Planning-Stage Assessment of Battery-Supported Regional Islanding: A South Australian Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2611.15364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power systems with high shares of renewable generation may face increased operational vulnerability under regional islanding caused by the loss of major inter-area transmission interfaces. This paper presents a planning-stage transmission-level assessment of regional islanding with battery storage, using a South Australian case study based on a synthetic representation of the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM). An interconnected planning baseline is compared with a stress test scenario involving complete regional-islanding over a 24-hour chronological horizon. The framework quantifies peak unserved power, total unserved energy, and the duration of unserved demand, while characterising battery redispatch and the synchronous inertia accessible to the subsystem.
item.dc:creator: Yunqi Wang, Nanduni Nimalsiri, Ghulam Mohy-ud-din, Thomas Brinsmead

item.title: SLyM: LLM-Driven Symbolic Lyapunov Function Discovery via Structure Proposal and Coefficient Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.15401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lyapunov functions are the cornerstone of stability analysis for dynamical systems, yet synthesizing a symbolic form remains difficult as no universal constructive algorithm exists. To address this challenge, we introduce SLyM, a framework that harnesses the knowledge and reasoning of large language models (LLMs) to discover symbolic Lyapunov functions. To avoid charging the LLM with ill-suited numerical generation, SLyM decomposes the construction into structure proposal and coefficient optimization: the LLM draws on its prior knowledge of Lyapunov constructions to propose the function structure, whose coefficients then follow from a convex program. Local-search structures are folded back into supervision, extending coverage to systems missed by the initial proposer. Across all benchmarks, SLyM consistently outperforms the evaluated neural, sum-of-squares, and generative baselines.
item.dc:creator: Zihao Fu, Xingchen Li, Keyou You

item.title: Quantitative Stability Region Estimation of Grid-Forming Inverters with Current Limiting via a State-Dependent Switched Energy Function
item.description: arXiv:2611.15466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With increasing renewable energy integration, grid-forming (GFM) inverters are becoming key components of future power systems. Compared with synchronous generators (SGs), GFM inverters have limited overcurrent capability and require current limiting. This can lead to switching between normal and current-limited operating modes under large disturbances, complicating synchronization dynamics and posing a longstanding challenge to existing transient-stability analysis methods. In this paper, a state-dependent switched (SdS) energy function theory is proposed for transient-stability analysis of GFM inverters with current limiting, whose dynamics can be abstracted as SdS nonlinear systems. Regional energy functions are constructed for individual operating modes and continuously matched at switching interfaces, yielding a continuous piecewise energy function. Hence, the derived conservative estimate of the stability region (region of attraction, ROA) spans different operating regions without prescribing subsequent current limiting activations and releases, a fundamental distinction from conventional methods using signal-mode energy functions. Techniques for incorporating damping energy are extended to the proposed framework to capture damping effects and further reduce the conservatism of the ROA estimates. The methodology applies to GFM inverters with different synchronization control loops and current-limiting strategies. Experiments on a physical GFM inverter under various grid contingencies validate the proposed quantitative transient stability assessment.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Zhang, Yang Wu

item.title: Estimation-Aware Control on Quadrotor State Manifolds via Anisotropic Covariance Filtering
item.description: arXiv:2611.15498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional nonlinear flight controllers operate under the implicit assumption of reliable, high-confidence state feedback. During transient sensing degradation or partial unobservability, state estimation uncertainty is frequently misinterpreted as physical tracking error, triggering aggressive and parasitic corrective inputs. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose a generalized Estimation-Aware (EA) control framework that directly incorporates real-time estimator confidence into control execution. By mapping the posterior error covariance $\mathbf{P}_{k\mid k}$ into an uncertainty-dependent modulation operator, the EA mechanism dynamically scales feedback authority, performing anisotropic attenuation along weakly observed state directions to prevent false error corrections. Validated across six distinct control paradigms, the proposed approach demonstrates substantial performance gains across all baselines. In particular, when integrated into an Incremental Nonlinear Dynamic Inversion (INDI) architecture, the EA mechanism reduces tracking and estimation errors by 24.34% and 33.24%, respectively, at a high flight speed of 10 m/s.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Engelsman, Itzik Klein

item.title: Adaptive Robust Output Regulation of Uncertain Linear Time-Varying Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.15500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies adaptive robust output regulation of linear time-varying systems with unknown constant parameters in both the plant and exosystem. The design is based on nonmonic differential relations for the ideal input. For general time-varying and periodic systems, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of nonmonic differential relations and construct them from the original system coefficients. Based on these relations, an adaptive controller is constructed using stable filters and a parameterized readout. Under suitable conditions on the filter and readout, the controller achieves exact regulation for finitely separable relation coefficients, including the affine parametric uncertainty treated in Byrnes--Isidori form. For coefficient families satisfying the approximation conditions, refining the approximation achieves any prescribed ultimate regulation accuracy with a fixed stabilization design, yielding practical regulation. Neither persistent excitation nor parameter convergence is required. Two numerical examples illustrate the regulation performance of the proposed controller. Overall, the framework includes earlier constructions based on finite separation of the ideal input or monic linear differential relations with finitely separable coefficients, and achieves exact robust regulation for a broader class of uncertain systems.
item.dc:creator: Jinmeng Zha, Zhen Zhang

item.title: Decentralised model predictive control of recurrent neural network models
item.description: arXiv:2611.15629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work proposes a decentralised nonlinear model predictive control algorithm for systems described by input-coupled recurrent neural network models. The proposed approach exploits closed-loop incremental input-to-state stability to design the local controllers and provide robustness to subsystem couplings. The resulting control scheme guarantees asymptotic convergence to a desired equilibrium while satisfying input and output constraints. Simulation results illustrate the performance of the proposed approach.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Ravasio, Marcello Farina, Andrea Ballarino

item.title: Transversal Passivity and Equilibrium Forces in Formation Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.15690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider controller synthesis for distance-constrained formations, aiming to stabilize the target formation manifold while sustaining admissible equilibrium edge forces. Using the newly introduced notion of transversal passivity, we encode the target formation shape, the prescribed edge lengths, and a subspace of internally balanced edge forces as the port target manifolds of the agents and the edge controller. The synthesis task is thereby reformulated as the joint design of a transversally passive edge controller and its output-target subspace. We then propose a general constructive realization of output-strictly transversally passive systems and specialize it to derive a dynamic edge controller that sustains admissible equilibrium edge forces. Through a compatibility analysis across the interconnection, we establish a closed-loop dissipation margin in terms of the controller parameters and prove local convergence of all agent and controller ports to their target manifolds. Numerical simulations validate the results.
item.dc:creator: Feng-Yu Yue, Daniel Zelazo

item.title: Assessing Data Center Hosting Capacity Considering Electromagnetic Transient Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.15704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hosting capacity is commonly assessed with steady-state optimization, which leaves the dynamic response of the data center and the grid at the resulting operating point untested. This paper assesses candidate data center capacities by coupling a unit commitment (UC) model with electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulation. During the capacity search, the UC model determines the economic dispatch for each tested data center capacity, and the resulting operating points are tested for settling with the generators committed online by the UC model and after a selected synchronous generator outage. Three nested capacities are obtained: the optimization-based steady-state capacity, the dynamic pre-outage capacity, and the post-outage dynamic capacity, each bounded by the previous one. On a test system with a detailed data center model, both dynamic capacities fall well below the optimization capacity, and the ranking of connection locations changes with the assessment stage and with the outage. In the most severe outage case at each candidate bus, the capacity is about 30% below the steady-state capacity. Thus, the dynamic response of the data center and the grid should be part of the hosting capacity assessment, and the comparison of connection locations should be made on the post-outage dynamic capacity.
item.dc:creator: Fan Jiang, Xingpeng Li

item.title: Quantifying the Cost of Restoring AC Feasibility for Approximate Optimal Power Flow Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.15706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power system operations rely on approximate solutions of the AC optimal power flow problem, most notably the DC optimal power flow used in security-constrained unit commitment and economic dispatch, while convex relaxations, machine learning surrogates, and other approximations are studied extensively in the academic literature. Because these approximations neglect or relax parts of the AC power flow equations, their solutions must be adjusted before dispatch; for example, the DC optimal power flow, which neglects transmission losses, reactive power, and voltage magnitude variations, is known to produce solutions that are always infeasible. The cost of this adjustment is not adequately understood. This paper proposes a method that quantifies, for any approximate solution, the minimum cost of the adjustments that restore AC feasibility, which is a lower bound on the cost of the heuristic adjustments used in practice. We apply it to the DC optimal power flow, the second-order cone and quadratic convex relaxations, and the AC optimal power flow solved to a loose relative tolerance of $10^{-4}$ instead of $10^{-8}$. Relative to the AC optimal power flow solution obtained from a local nonlinear optimization solver, and even with the minimum adjustment, the DC optimal power flow requires adjusting, on average, generators that account for 15.6% of total generation capacity and incurs a 1.10% cost increase; the convex relaxations require more adjustment (17.2% and 16.9%) but smaller cost increases (0.68% and 0.78%); and the loose-tolerance AC optimal power flow requires 6.1% and incurs 0.42%. These results indicate significant value in operating markets directly on the AC optimal power flow, which avoids the distortion of the dispatch and prices caused by heuristic feasibility restoration.
item.dc:creator: Sanjay Johnson, Sungho Shin

item.title: Scalable Reference Electrical Architectures for Modern Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2611.15712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of cloud computing, artificial intelligence (AI), and high-performance computing is driving the deployment of data centers with electrical demands ranging from tens of megawatts to multi-gigawatt campuses, creating significant challenges for utility interconnection and power system planning. This paper presents scalable, vendor-neutral reference electrical architectures for colocation, hyperscale, and AI data centers. The proposed framework integrates modular Power PODs, hierarchical HV/MV/LV distribution, standby generation, uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), battery energy storage systems (BESS), and scalable utility interfaces into a unified planning methodology. Three representative Power POD configurations are developed to support systematic capacity expansion while maintaining consistent electrical topology and equipment sizing. The proposed architectures facilitate utility interconnection studies, equipment demand forecasting, transmission planning, and grid infrastructure assessment, providing an open and reproducible benchmark for evaluating the impacts of large-scale data center deployment on future power systems.
item.dc:creator: Kiran Kumar Challa (Joann), Yan (Joann), Zhou, Kumarsinh Jhala

item.title: Adaptive Model Predictive Control for Damping IBR-Induced SSOs
item.description: arXiv:2611.15742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an adaptive model predictive control (MPC) approach to damp sub-synchronous oscillations (SSOs) induced by grid-following (GFL) inverter-based resources (IBRs). Unlike traditional model predictive controller designed considering the nominal plant that may not perform well in other conditions, we use plants that alter with changing operating point. To capture the plant dynamics, we use recursive least squares (RLS) based system identification with variable forgetting factor. This approach allows us to discount past data and avoid bias caused by large transient outliers while performing system identification. We present a proof of the convergence of the model parameters in the presence of finite outliers. We propose to update the model inside the MPC optimization problem periodically after a predetermined time interval instead of each sampling instant since the operating point changes slowly in a practical power system. The MPC design allows us to directly impose constraints on control inputs so that the IBR current limits are respected. Our approach also addresses the issue of unavailability of IBR models. We show the accuracy of the system identification and the superior performance of the proposed controller on the modified IEEE $4$-machine system and the modified IEEE $68$-bus system as compared with the traditional MPC.
item.dc:creator: Fiaz Hossain, Nilanjan Ray Chaudhuri, Constantino M. Lagoa

item.title: Robust Safe Control Under Uncertainty: Estimation, Contraction, and Regret Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2611.15776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Disturbance uncertainty requires safety filters based on control barrier functions (CBFs) to leave a robustness margin, which can alter the nominal control input and degrade closed-loop performance. This paper studies safety and the resulting performance loss for discrete-time nonlinear systems with additive disturbances and polytopic input constraints. We develop a causal disturbance observer and construct two robust barrier conditions. The first uses a time-dependent bound on the estimation error. The second uses a constant margin when the disturbance increments are uniformly bounded and moves the requirement on the initial error from the online filter to an explicit initialization condition. For affine barriers, both filters are quadratic programs. We bound their input deviations from an oracle filter with access to the current disturbance and derive sufficient conditions for uniform contraction of the oracle closed loop. The contraction analysis accounts for state-dependent actuation, unmatched disturbances, and active physical input limits. Combining the sensitivity and contraction estimates gives finite-time dynamic regret bounds that quantify the effects of observer convergence, disturbance variation, and robustness margins. With sublinear cumulative certified disturbance variation and observer innovation error, the bounds yield sublinear regret.
item.dc:creator: Changrui Liu, Liang Wu, Anil Alan, Shengling Shi, Bart De Schutter

item.title: Quasi-Static Fault-Tolerant Feedback Control of a Quadrotor Carrying a Slung Payload under Rotor Failure
item.description: arXiv:2611.15787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a nonlinear control law for a slung payload system (SPS) consisting of a quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) carrying a slung payload. We propose a fault-tolerant control (FTC) design for the case of a complete single-rotor failure, i.e., only three functioning propellers. The failure is not modeled as a disturbance to be handled by estimation. Rather, we model the faulty SPS in control-affine form and design a quasi-static feedback law directly for the faulty dynamics. The controller achieves local exponential convergence of the payload position to a geometric path in space, rather than tracking a timed reference trajectory. Moreover, the transverse dynamics are exponentially stable, and the path-following manifold is rendered controlled invariant by feedback. Controlled invariance allows motion along the path to be prescribed independently through a tangential command while the state stays on the path-following manifold. The UAV body angular velocity remains bounded under bounded applied torque despite the failure. To validate the control design, numerical simulations apply the controller derived from the faulty SPS model in coordinates to the coordinate-free SPS model. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/qs-sl/.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Al Lawati, Adeel Akhtar

item.title: Impact of Grid-Interactive Data Center Microgrids on Grid Reliability
item.description: arXiv:2611.15903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional data centers, operating as passive loads with standby backup resources, present significant challenges for grid integration due to their scale, rapid load fluctuations, and limited operational flexibility. This article investigates the transformative potential of grid-interactive data center microgrids, which integrate battery energy storage, on-site generation, and intelligent microgrid controllers to actively support both facility and grid operations. The proposed simulation framework enables the study comparing conventional and grid-interactive architectures under a range of steady-state and contingency scenarios. Results reveal that grid-interactive microgrids can substantially reduce peak grid demand, improve voltage stability, and improve system reliability especially when data center and system load peaks coincide. The findings highlight the critical role of coordinated resource management in enabling the reliable and efficient integration of large data center loads, and provide a practical methodology for assessing their system-level impacts.
item.dc:creator: Kiran Kumar Challa, Kumarsinh Jhala

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Target Jerk Estimation in Interceptor Homing Phase
item.description: arXiv:2611.15923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate the use of reinforcement meta-learning (meta-RL) to optimize a target jerk estimation policy, which is then used as the target acceleration rate of change in the propagation model of an unscented Kalman filter (UKF). The policy is learned through simulated engagements of a terminal phase high-altitude endoatmospheric interception of a highly maneuverable target, with a hit-to-kill accuracy requirement. As benchmarks, we tuned both a standard UKF and an interacting multiple model (IMM) filter, where the IMM uses a different constant jerk assumption for each model. The benchmarks and the proposed augmented UKF with the target jerk policy are tested in a 6-DOF simulation environment, which has sufficient fidelity to capture most factors relevant to guidance, navigation, and flight control. The augmented UKF demonstrates significant improvement in target interception rate, with more challenging maneuvers giving the largest performance differential. The meta-RL jerk policy is then tested on an expanded engagement scenario, with increased initial state estimate uncertainty and novel target maneuvers, demonstrating that the meta-RL policy generalizes well to conditions not seen during optimization.
item.dc:creator: Brian Gaudet, Dalton Durant, Roberto Furfaro

item.title: Model Predictive Control on Analogue Hardware: A Dual-flow Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.15934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current Model Predictive Control (MPC) implementations are predominantly digital and, despite offering high precision and flexibility, often face challenges with ultra-low latency and hardware certification for safety-critical applications. We present an approach for solving the Quadratic Program (QP) of MPC using a continuous-time neural ordinary differential equation in the dual space. We obtain the solution to these QPs by mapping the differential equation's equilibrium point back to the primal space via a nonlinear transformation. The underlying dual-flow dynamics operate natively on analogue hardware. We validate this approach by demonstrating the hardware implementation of linear MPC on "The Analog Thing" analogue computer. Finally, we extend the framework to nonlinear MPC with successive linearisation, broadening the applicability beyond linear systems.
item.dc:creator: Nikilesh Ramesh, Ross Drummond, Pablo R Baldivieso-Monasterios, Morgan Jones, Yuanbo Nie

item.title: Cooperative Learning of Shared Latent Dynamics for Distributed Online Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.15953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study networked agents that must agree on a decision minimizing the sum of their local costs, where each cost contains unmeasurable stochastic parameters that evolve with linear but unknown dynamics shared by all agents. Each agent receives only finitely many noisy gradient measurements and must then keep tracking the moving minimizer. Our scheme reconstructs the parameters from windows of gradients, learns the shared dynamics cooperatively by averaging instrumental-variable moment matrices over the network, and tracks the minimizer by gradient tracking on forecast gradients. We bound the error of every agent in learning the dynamics and in tracking the minimizer, and show that the learning error, and through it the tracking error, decreases with the number of agents. We demonstrate the approach on two case studies.
item.dc:creator: Shivanshu Tripathi, Maziar Raissi

item.title: Data-center growth impacts household electricity costs more through wholesale prices than through grid reinforcement
item.description: arXiv:2611.16095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid data-center expansion is raising concerns about electricity affordability, yet how the costs of serving these large new loads reach residential customers remains poorly understood. Here, we quantify the potential impact of 371 announced Texas data-center projects, totaling 38.9 GW by 2030, on residential electricity costs by linking power system expansion, wholesale electricity markets, transmission reinforcement, and retail cost allocation. We find that accommodating this demand increases modeled residential electricity costs in one representative case by 1.64 cents/kWh, with 68% arising from higher wholesale electricity prices and 32% from regulated transmission charges. Allowing new gas generation near data centers reduces the 2023 residential cost increase to 0.92 cents/kWh, whereas excluding data centers from the transmission cost-sharing base raises it to 1.87 cents/kWh. These findings reveal that the residential cost burden of data-center growth is driven primarily by wholesale electricity price increases, rather than direct transmission investment costs, and depends critically on generation siting, infrastructure planning, and cost allocation.
item.dc:creator: Lingdong Zhou, Wenjia Xia, Jiyu Wang, Fei Ding, Xiangqi Zhu

item.title: GridForge: A Tractable Network-Flow Method for Constructing Open, Continental-Scale Synthetic Power Grids
item.description: arXiv:2611.16222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal of this paper is to construct open, continental-scale synthetic transmission grids with an optimization method that stays tractable. Security restrictions keep models of the real grid out of open research and machine-learning datasets, and optimization-based construction is hard at scale: the number of candidate lines grows combinatorially, so electrically faithful methods prune the candidates in advance. This paper presents GridForge, which keeps every bus pair within physical length limits as a candidate, selects lines with Garver's length-weighted network-flow linear program instead of binary decisions, and resizes them with a sequential direct-current (DC) power flow. Two stages of 13 regional networks are evaluated. Their node-degree distributions are nearly as strongly log-linear as those of the real Eastern and Western Interconnections ($R^2$ of 0.92 to 0.98 against 0.971 and 0.981), although the areas under the fitted lines differ from the real ones by 39.9% on average. On the upper Midwest and Tennessee Valley footprints, resizing lowers the DC power-flow loss from 5.89% to 4.14% and from 14.55% to 7.05%, and the DC optimal power-flow loss from 4.03% to 2.02% and from 5.54% to 2.47%. Without relaxing any line limit, the DC optimal power flow is feasible in 78.81% and 0.82% of the scenarios. Most lines are built at 69 kV. The models span 250 to 78,484 buses, were built on single machines, and are freely redistributable.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan M. Snodgrass, Thomas J. Overbye, Christopher L. DeMarco, Bernard C. Lesieutre

item.title: DER Aggregators in Wholesale Electricity Markets: A Hybrid Mean-Field Framework with Endogenous Price Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.16230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of distributed energy resources (DERs), including rooftop solar and energy storage, is transforming the grid edge, where customer-side assets increasingly interact with the broader power grid. DER aggregators, entities that coordinate the actions of many small-scale DERs, play a key role in this transformation. This paper presents a hybrid Mean-Field Control (MFC) and Mean-Field Game (MFG) framework for integrating DER aggregators into wholesale electricity markets. Unlike traditional approaches that treat market prices as exogenous, our model captures the feedback between aggregators' collective actions and electricity prices. The MFC component optimizes DER operations within each aggregator, while the MFG models strategic interactions among multiple aggregators. To account for various uncertainties, we incorporate reinforcement learning, which allows aggregators to learn optimal bidding strategies in dynamic market conditions. We prove the existence and uniqueness of a mean-field equilibrium and validate the framework through a case study of the Oahu Island power system. Results show that our approach reduces price volatility and improves market efficiency, offering a scalable and decentralized solution for DER integration in wholesale markets.
item.dc:creator: Jun He, Andrew L. Liu

item.title: On Energy-Based Modelling for Fluidic Excitable Neurons
item.description: arXiv:2611.16389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by the potential of pneumatic excitable devices in soft robotics, this paper develops an energy-based, domain-agnostic equivalent of the Hodgkin-Huxley modelling framework using bond graph theory. The proposed model is used to guide the design of a pneumatic excitable neuron. The potential of this approach is illustrated through the design of a pneumatic half-center oscillator, an essential building block for rhythmic neuromorphic behaviours.
item.dc:creator: Robin Wroblowski, Brent Michiels, Benjamin Gorissen, Rodolphe Sepulchre

item.title: A Joint LLM and Optimization Agent Solution for Drone Scheduling in Victim Search Missions
item.description: arXiv:2611.16524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Victim search in wilderness areas is time-critical. Drones enable rapid area search, but scheduling them is challenging because victims may continue moving, detection results are uncertain, and effective decisions must combine structured mission information with unstructured contextual clues and domain knowledge. To address this, we propose an agent-aided drone scheduling system. The system employs an agent at the ground control station (GCS) to coordinate multiple drones over successive search cycles. In each cycle, the agent applies a scheduling policy that combines a large language model (LLM) for reasoning about where to search with an optimizer for determining how to dispatch the drones under energy constraints. Simulation results show that the proposed system consistently completes the victim-search mission, whereas none of the six non-LLM baselines does so and direct LLM scheduling is considerably less reliable. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/1643204431/llm-uav-victim-search.
item.dc:creator: Yinghao Zhang, Yalin Liu, Hong-Ning Dai, Yan Zhang, Qubeijian Wang, Bishenghui Tao, Yaohan Li

item.title: Incremental Model Predictive Control for Reference Tracking of Nonlinear Anesthesia Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.16537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anesthesia dynamics are commonly described by Wiener models, consisting of linear dynamics followed by a static nonlinearity. This nonlinear output complicates the derivation of theoretical guarantees on closed-loop stability and convergence. Model Predictive Control (MPC) is particularly suitable for anesthesia control, as it explicitly accounts for constraints in the control design. In this paper, we propose an incremental MPC formulation for tracking a desired reference. The proposed approach exploits the structure of the nonlinear output equation to reformulate the control problem within a linear framework. An incremental model is then employed to avoid the explicit computation of steady states and inputs, which may be inaccurate in the presence of model uncertainties. The proposed controller is evaluated through simulations involving 1000 virtual patients and compared with a benchmark MPC formulation. Results show improved steady-state reference tracking while maintaining satisfactory disturbance rejection.
item.dc:creator: Maxim Raymond, Kaouther Moussa, Teodoro Alamo, Mirko Fiacchini, Jimmy Lauber

item.title: Can STATCOM and UPS-Based Voltage Support Mitigate Fault-Induced Reductions in AI Data Center Grid Power Draw?
item.description: arXiv:2611.16569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are rapidly increasing in number and capacity. These large electronic loads are interfaced through power electronic devices and can sharply reduce grid power intake during fault-induced voltage sags. Disturbances exceeding equipment ride-through capabilities may also trigger protective disconnection, posing risks to power system security. Static synchronous compensators (STATCOMs) and appropriately controlled AIDC uninterruptible power supply (UPS) rectifiers can provide reactive power support during voltage sags. This paper compares the individual and combined effectiveness of STATCOM and UPS-based voltage support in mitigating fault-induced reductions in grid power intake through electromagnetic transient simulations of a 1 GW AIDC connected to an IEEE nine-bus system. Simulation results show that STATCOM support better preserves short-term intake in milder tested faults, whereas UPS coordination maintains rectifier operation under deeper sags by reducing active intake to reserve reactive current capacity. Combined support improves auxiliary load retention and recovery in selected cases. However, severe tested sags still cause substantial grid-demand reductions even with combined support.
item.dc:creator: Ziang Liu, Yimeng Liu, Francis Yunhe Hou

item.title: Energy system device sizing under closed-loop operation with imperfect forecasts
item.description: arXiv:2611.16699v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The value of renewable energy devices depends on their operation, which must adapt to weather and demand using limited, imperfect forecasts that update over time. Conventional energy systems planning practices assume unlimited foresight in a single-level formulation, potentially leading to long-term investment in suboptimal device sizes. Accounting for realistic operation corresponds to a bi-level problem: the upper level selects device sizes, while the lower level contains closed-loop operation under evolving forecasts. We solve this problem using backpropagation MPC (BP-MPC), a gradient-based method, with a deterministic MPC as the lower-level controller. Using forecast errors generated by a parameterized martingale model of forecast evolution, we investigate how forecast accuracy affects the benefits of operation-aware energy systems planning and the resulting device sizes. In a case study of an energy system comprising photovoltaics, a battery, a heat pump, and thermal storage with uncertain weather and energy demands, accounting for closed-loop operation yields higher average cost savings as forecast error increases. The resulting designs achieve these savings by progressively shifting investment from battery storage to solar generation and thermal storage, which buffers forecast mismatches.
item.dc:creator: Cara Koepele, Kevin Wallington, Georgios Mavromatidis, John Lygeros

item.title: Velocity-Free Funnel Control of Euler-Lagrange Systems: An Artificial-Delay Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.16707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical funnel control keeps the tracking error within a prescribed, time-varying envelope by increasing the feedback gain as the error approaches the boundary. For mechanical systems, this guarantee typically relies on velocity measurements. We show that it can be retained for fully actuated Euler--Lagrange systems using only position measurements. The proposed controller replaces the velocity error with a difference quotient of the position error over a fixed delay, while preserving the classical unbounded gain. It requires no plant model, reference derivatives, observer, or filter states. The central challenge is to reconcile the averaging inherent in delayed feedback with a gain that can grow without bound near the funnel boundary. We resolve this by establishing an a priori bound on the gain along closed-loop trajectories, independent of the delay. This bound yields a computable delay threshold that guarantees tracking within the prescribed funnel and boundedness of all closed-loop signals. The threshold depends only on bounds on the inertia, forces, and reference. Simulations demonstrate tracking accuracy comparable to full-state funnel control and tolerance of delays substantially longer than certified. With quantized position measurements, the controller also requires substantially less torque than an existing derivative-free funnel controller.
item.dc:creator: Chayan Kumar Paul, Pushpak Jagtap

item.title: Structure-Preserving Learning for Nonlinear Nonholonomic Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.16796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning the dynamics of mechanical systems subject to nonlinear nonholonomic constraints is challenging, as data-driven models may violate the underlying physical constraints, leading to inconsistent predictions. To address this problem, we develop a constraint-preserving learning framework based on the Lagrange-d'Alembert-Chetaev equations and tangency to the constraint submanifold, which together define an affine space of admissible accelerations. Using the kinetic-energy metric and the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, we construct a metric projector and the corresponding Chetaev correction. Embedding this geometric structure directly into a Gaussian process prior ensures that both prior and posterior dynamics satisfy the acceleration constraints exactly. We characterize the resulting reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), derive an adapted-coordinate representation, and establish nonexpansiveness and consistency transfer. Numerical experiments on a three-dimensional directional flocking system with up to 50 agents demonstrate exact constraint preservation and robustness to constraint-incompatible observations.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Beckers, Anthony Bloch, Leonardo Colombo

item.title: FlatSeek: LLM-Driven Symbolic Discovery of Flat Outputs via Backward Data Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differential flatness enables efficient planning and control, but discovering explicit flat outputs for general nonlinear systems remains difficult due to the lack of general methods and supervised data. We propose FlatSeek, a framework combining backward data generation with task-specific large language model (LLM) training. By reversing the defining reconstruction of flatness, we generate system-flat-output pairs with known certificates, then fine-tune an LLM to propose symbolic flat-output candidates for unseen dynamics. On literature and synthetic benchmarks, FlatSeek outperforms both the traditional symbolic methods and the untuned reference models in flat-output discovery success, and uncovers alternative symbolic flat outputs not reported in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Zihao Fu, Xingchen Li, Keyou You

item.title: Quantum Network Flows That Solve Linear Equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.16808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a distributed quantum network flow for solving linear equations from locally stored row data. Local pumping enforces each node's equation constraint, while neighboring registers interact through swaps. The node marginals obey an exact, closed flow combining consensus with local constraint enforcement. For consistent equations, all node states converge exponentially to a common state supported on the solution space; a unique solution yields full-network convergence to the product solution state. For inconsistent equations of full column rank, scaled encoding and readout recover the least-squares solution through successive large-gain and small-scale limits. For consistent systems, the marginal convergence rate is nondecreasing and concave in the swap gain, approaching a graph-independent limit for fixed local dissipators. Its leading finite-gain correction couples graph topology and row placement through the Laplacian pseudoinverse, enabling semidefinite optimization of edge rates under a fixed total swap-rate budget. For invertible systems, a dissipative HHL-type construction using the same pumping law provides a comparison of solution-state encodings, decay rates, and row-update locality under squared-row-norm pumping. Numerical examples are provided to validate the presented results.
item.dc:creator: Chengyang Jiang, Zihao Ren, Lei Wang, Guodong Shi

item.title: Adjacent Heat Transfer Effects Can Bias Savings Estimates When Controlling Only Part of a Multi-Zone Building
item.description: arXiv:2611.16866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Field demonstrations of advanced heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning control often operate a few thermal zones within a larger building and report savings for those zones alone. A recent theorem showed that this practice overestimates whole-building savings, because heat drawn from the neighboring zones is paid for by their equipment and is not counted. The error grows with the thermal conductance between the controlled and uncontrolled zones, with how much colder the controlled zones run over the test, and with the price of the heat their neighbors supply. For one controlled zone with one neighbor, a single thermal price, and slowly changing prices, the relative error reduces to the ratio of two conductances, a screening number that can be evaluated from the two conductances before a demonstration begins. This paper tests how far that reduction can be taken. A two-story house with one thermal zone per floor is simulated over a 90-day heating season in West Lafayette, Indiana, with receding-horizon model predictive control on the first floor and setpoint control on the second, under four combinations of electricity tariff (time-of-use or flat) and heating plant (heat pump or electric resistance). The exact correction from the theorem recovers the true savings in every case, and the full theorem, evaluated from the controlled zone's temperatures, the prices, and the building parameters, reproduces the measured relative error in every case. The conductance ratio bounds that error from above in all four cases, tightly under a flat tariff, within 3%, and loosely under a time-of-use tariff, where most of the controller's savings come from shifting load through the thermal mass rather than from lowering the temperature.
item.dc:creator: Arash J. Khabbazi, Kevin J. Kircher

item.title: A New Analytical Method and Interpretation of Loss-of-Load Counts
item.description: arXiv:2611.16888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper establishes the relationship between loss-of-load expectation (LOLE) and loss-of-load frequency (LOLF). We show why LOLE generally does not measure distinct-event frequency, mean event duration, or shortage magnitude. We identify conditions under which peak-based LOLE admits a frequency interpretation as the expected count of deficient daily peaks per horizon and distinguish this quantity from LOLF. We also derive an analytical formulation for frequency-and-duration indices that combines a convolution-derived generation probability-and-frequency model with chronological load changes. Under stationary generation, it uses the prescribed load profile directly, without constructing a separate load model or discretizing load magnitudes. Studies using generation and load data from the 24-bus IEEE RTS reveal different event frequencies and mean event durations at identical peak-based LOLE, motivating their separate assessment. Numerical comparisons demonstrate the accuracy advantage of the proposed analytical calculation over the conventional analytical implementations, quantifying the LOLF errors incurred by load discretization.
item.dc:creator: Aidan Looney, Chanan Singh, Le Xie

item.title: Mode-in-Variance Participation Factors under Stochastic Excitation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates how the dynamic modes of a power system contribute to the stationary variance of its variables under continuous stochastic excitation. Using a modal decomposition of the covariance matrix, the variance of each state or algebraic variable can be resolved into components associated with individual modal responses and their interactions. These components are shown to correspond to within-mode variance and cross-modal covariance, respectively, and the corresponding normalized contributions are termed mode-in-variance participation factors (PFs). The proposed PFs can be used to identify modes governing the variability of important system quantities such as frequency and voltage, quantify the effect of modal interactions, and reveal control dynamics that can be targeted to reduce their stochastic variability. These capabilities are demonstrated through case studies based on the Kundur two-area and IEEE 39-bus systems.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Pinheiro, Liya Huang, Georgios Tzounas

item.title: Improved Single-Input Space Vector for DC-Biased Sinusoidal Current Control in Battery Cyclers
item.description: arXiv:2611.16926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents improvements to the single-input space vector (SISV) concept for current control in a battery cycler based on a two-phase interleaved buck converter. The cycler is controlled to output a dc-biased sinusoidal current, enabling investigation of second-harmonic ripple effects on lithium-ion cell aging. A modified SISV generation scheme is introduced to track current references containing both dc and sinusoidal components, and an impedance-angle compensation method is proposed to decouple the d and q control axes without disturbing dc tracking. A dq phase-portrait visualization method is also introduced to evaluate transient performance for both SISV and proportional-integral-resonant (PIR) control methods. Simulation and experimental results validate dc-biased sinusoidal current tracking using PIR control and SISV control with different decoupling schemes. The phase-portrait framework allows for straightforward evaluation of transient performance for both SISV and PIR control methods and supports controller tuning to obtain desired trajectories. The results demonstrate the feasibility of SISV-based current control as an alternative to PIR control for battery-cycler applications. The proposed improvements support the development of battery cyclers capable of controlling both dc and sinusoidal current components.
item.dc:creator: Manveer Aujla, Philip Lewoc, Harminderjit S. Toor, Ahmad Ali, Caniggia Viana, Narayan C. Kar

item.title: A Modulation Strategy for Bidirectional Integrated Onboard and Wireless EV Charging
item.description: arXiv:2611.16950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated electric vehicle chargers reduce cost by sharing power conversion hardware between the onboard charger (OBC) and the wireless charger (WC). A previously proposed dual active bridge (DAB)-based OBC/WC shares the rectification stage between the OBC and WC; however, the modulation required to realize its wireless operation has not yet been reported. This paper details a modulation strategy that enables the operation of the integrated OBC/WC topology. Differential-mode operation is used for the OBC, and common-mode operation is used for the WC. In OBC mode, the shared full-bridge produces differential-mode voltage for wired power transfer while ideally generating zero common-mode voltage on the wireless charging path. In WC mode, the same full-bridge produces common-mode voltage for wireless power transfer while ideally generating zero differential-mode voltage on the onboard charging path. The method preserves conventional DAB phase-shift power control and enables bidirectional power transfer in wired and wireless charging modes without additional contactors. Design considerations for the OBC transformer and WC coils are derived based on the resulting square-wave voltage amplitudes. Offline PLECS simulations demonstrate power tracking and decoupled charger operation at $\pm$7.4 kW. Hardware-in-the-loop simulations using a PLECS RT Box and an external Texas Instruments microcontroller further validate the proposed modulation method.
item.dc:creator: Manveer Aujla, Gavin Feher, Caniggia Viana

item.title: Survivability Guarantees for Delayed Serial Supply Chains under Demand Shocks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When demand exceeds the maximum production capacity of a supply chain, it can be satisfied only for a finite time, determined by the inventory stored along the chain. Existing control methods ensure indefinite constraint satisfaction under bounded demand, but provide no guarantees on how long a supply chain can withstand a shock in which demand goes beyond production capacity. We address this gap for a serial supply chain with transportation delays and flow constraints. Under a specified flow policy, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the inventory distribution that guarantee a prescribed lower bound on the exit time from the set where demand is served. We use these conditions to compute inventory targets that minimize holding costs via a quadratic program. Then, we propose a two-mode controller that builds reserves under ordinary demand and depletes them during the shock. Simulations illustrate this approach.
